Sequential Sample Size for a Fixed-Width Interval for a Mean Under Two-Phase Sampling

Source: R/ss_seq_two_phase.R
ss_seq_two_phase.Rd

Evaluates, at the data in hand, a sequential stopping rule for a two-phase design: the proxy measurement is available on every unit of a pool, the costly target measurement is added to units drawn at random from the pool a few at a time, and sampling stops at the first number of labeled units, at or after a minimum of m0, at which the confidence interval from ci_two_phase has a half-width no larger than half_width. Unlike ss_aipe_two_phase, the rule needs no planning values for the target's standard deviation or its correlation with the proxy: the data supply both as they accrue. It follows ss_seq_c in its stopping rule, in the half_width and alpha_level arguments, and in the rows it returns (with the sizes named for the labeled units), and like it keeps no state: call it again after each batch. It differs from ss_seq_c() in three ways: it takes the data rather than summary statistics; it has no quantile argument, since its criterion is the half-width of the interval ci_two_phase reports, which uses the t quantile (the default of ss_seq_c()); and its minimum m0 counts labeled units and defaults to 30 rather than ss_seq_c()'s 10 per group, because the slope as well as the variance must be estimated before the rule can be trusted.

Usage

ss_seq_two_phase(y, x, x_unlabeled, half_width, alpha_level = 0.05, m0 = 30)

Arguments

y

The target measurement on the units labeled so far.

x

The proxy measurement on the same units, aligned with y.

x_unlabeled

The proxy measurement on the units of the pool not yet labeled.

half_width

The target half-width \(h\) of the 100(1 - 2\(\alpha\))% confidence interval, in the units of the target. For a noninferiority or equivalence decision at bounds \(\pm\delta\), ss_seq_c explains why \(\delta/2\) is the usual choice.

alpha_level

One-sided rate per bound; the interval is at confidence level 1 - 2\(\alpha\). Default 0.05 (a 90% interval), as in ss_seq_c.

m0

The minimum number of labeled units before the rule may stop, default 30. The early variance and slope estimates are unstable, and a rule allowed to stop on them stops too early too often.

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_tbl) with rows stop (1 when the rule is met, so labeling stops; 0 to continue), half_width_current (the half-width of the interval now), half_width_target, n_labeled_current (the labeled units used, after any with a missing value are set aside, as in ci_two_phase), n_labeled_projected, and n_pool (\(M\)).

Details

The rule. With \(n\) labeled units and a pool of \(M\), sampling stops when \(n \ge m_0\) and $$t_{1-\alpha,\, n-2} \left\{\frac{S_e^2}{n} + \frac{\hat b^2 S_X^2}{M}\right\}^{1/2} \le h,$$ the left side being the half-width of the regression interval of ci_two_phase at confidence level 1 - 2\(\alpha\) (\(S_e^2\) the residual mean square of the target on the proxy, \(\hat b\) the slope, \(S_X^2\) the proxy's variance over the pool). This carries the fixed-width sequential approach of Chow and Robbins (1965), which ss_seq_c applies to a contrast, over to the two-phase interval. Labeled units must be added at random from the units not yet labeled, so that at every step they remain a simple random subsample of the pool. In an evaluation of a system whose outputs an automated judge labels, for example, a human assessor labels outputs drawn at random from those the judge has labeled until the rule says stop.

The projection. n_labeled_projected is the number of labeled units at which the rule would be met if the current estimates held, from the normal approximation \(n = S_e^2 / \{(h / z_{1-\alpha})^2 - \hat b^2 S_X^2 / M\}\), the same device ss_seq_c uses: a guide to how much further to go, not a commitment. When the current estimates say that labeling every unit of the pool but one (the interval needs at least one unit with the proxy alone) would not reach the target, the projection is NA with a warning: the pool, not the labeling, is then the constraint.

A constant target, or one the proxy reproduces exactly. While every labeled unit has the same target value (for example, a binary target that has been 1 on every unit so far), the residual variation and the slope are both zero, and the interval would have zero width. While the target is an exact linear function of the proxy on the labeled units (for example, a binary judge and a binary human label that have agreed on every unit so far), the residual variation is zero and the width of the interval would come from the size of the pool alone. In both cases the rule could stop on no evidence, so the function stops with an error asking for more labeled units, whether or not the rule would have been met, as it does while the proxy is constant on them. The residual variance is taken to be zero when it is no larger than .Machine$double.eps times the variance of the target on the labeled units, which allows for rounding error.

Coverage. The stopping size is random and the interval at stopping is computed as though it had been fixed, so its coverage is not guaranteed in finite samples; it can fall short of nominal when \(n\) at stopping is small, or for a bounded target (a proportion, for example) whose variance depends on its mean. The minimum m0 is the guard against the worst of this, and a simulation of the whole procedure in a plausible population is the check for a given design.

References

Chow, Y. S., & Robbins, H. (1965). On the asymptotic theory of fixed-width sequential confidence intervals for the mean. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 36(2), 457–462. doi:10.1214/aoms/1177700156

Neyman, J. (1938). Contribution to the theory of sampling human populations. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 33(201), 101–116. doi:10.1080/01621459.1938.10503378

See also

ss_seq_c, the sequential rule for a contrast; ci_two_phase; ss_aipe_two_phase for a design fixed in advance from planning values.

Other sequential estimation: ss_seq_c(), ss_seq_c_sensitivity()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# A proxy is available on a pool of 5,000 units; the target has been
# measured on a random 40 of them so far. Is a 90% interval with
# half-width 1 reached?
set.seed(113)
proxy  <- rnorm(5000, mean = 50, sd = 10)
target <- 20 + 0.6 * proxy + rnorm(5000, sd = 5)
order  <- sample(5000)
first  <- order[1:40]
ss_seq_two_phase(y = target[first], x = proxy[first],
                 x_unlabeled = proxy[-first], half_width = 1)
#>  term                value
#>  stop                0    
#>  half_width_current  1.124
#>  half_width_target   1    
#>  n_labeled_current   40   
#>  n_labeled_projected 49   
#>  n_pool              5000 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 90%

# Not yet; the projection suggests about 50. After labeling the next 30
# units at random:
first <- order[1:70]
ss_seq_two_phase(y = target[first], x = proxy[first],
                 x_unlabeled = proxy[-first], half_width = 1)
#>  term                value
#>  stop                1    
#>  half_width_current  0.896
#>  half_width_target   1    
#>  n_labeled_current   70   
#>  n_labeled_projected 70   
#>  n_pool              5000 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 90%
